gloss: the sense must be ‘slackens,’ i.e. abates, his course. The word *bait*, ‘to stop on a journey for refreshment’ (cognate with *bite*), is not very dignified now, but it may not have been open to this objection in Milton’s time.
a picture of the world in the ‘Silver Age,’ when the government was patriarchal (“under paternal rule”); that of iron soon (24) begins (Richardson).
i.e. Nimrod. In what follows M. is giving expression to his own republican feelings, and his dislike of a monarchy. Nimrod, he says, was the first to claim sovereign power over his fellow-men.

the description of Nimrod in Gen. x. 9, “He was a mighty hunter before the Lord,” has been explained in two ways: literally, according to the obvious sense of the English rendering; figuratively, as meaning that he was a great conqueror. Men, not beasts, were his prey.

lemma: from rebellion shall derive his name
gloss: alluding to the incorrect notion that Nimrod is connected with the Heb. root *marad*, ‘to rebel.’ Of course, it suits Milton’s sarcastic purpose to imply that the first king in history was himself but a rebel.

cf. the account of the building of the Tower of Babel in Gen. xi. 2–9. M. follows the original very closely. The Bible does not directly associate Nimrod with the building of the Tower of Babel; it only states (Gen. x. 10) that Babel was one of his capitals.

lemma: The plain, wherein a black bituminous gurge
gloss: *the plain*, i.e. in Mesopotamia, bordered by the Euphrates. *bituminous*. The mineral pitch called bitumen (or *asphalt*) abounded in Babylonia, and was employed, it is thought, in the buildings of the city of Babylon.

“This ‘bituminous gurge’ the poet calls ‘the mouth of hell,’ not strictly speaking, but by the same sort of figure by which the ancient poets called Taenarus or Avernus the jaws and gate of Hell” (Newton).
cf. Gen. xi. 9, “Therefore is the name of it called Babel,” where the margin has, “That is, Confusion.”
aiming at subduing; commonly used, like Lat. *affectare*, with a direct accusative of the thing aimed at.
i.e. Ham, the father of Canaan. Cf. Gen. ix. 21–25, especially verse 25, “And he said, Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren.”
i.e. eastward of. The word *ibri*, whence *Hebrew*, which was first used of Abraham (Gen. xiv. 13), signifies ‘living across,’ i.e. across, or east of, the Euphrates.

*Ur*, the capital of southern Chaldea, and a great commercial mart. But from the reference to Haran we may conjecture that M. supposed Ur to be in Upper Mesopotamia, i.e. at least 400 miles north of its real site.

the four boundaries are: (1) the town (or district) of Hamath, in Upper Syria, lying in the valley of the Orontes. (2) The Desert of Zin, forming part of the southern frontier of the Holy Land. (3) Mt Hermon, ‘the lofty peak.’ (4) The “western sea,” i.e. the Mediterranean.

lemma: Mount Carmel: here the double-founted stream
gloss: Mt Carmel is one of the most striking geographical features of Palestine. *double-founted*; probably an allusion to the old belief that the Jordan, in its upper course, was formed by the union of two streams thought to give the river its name; these were the Dan and the Jor.
cf. Gal. iii. 9, “So then they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.” The historical allusion in the lines is, of course, to Jacob’s going down to Egypt at the bidding of Joseph.
i.e. Pharaoh. Compare Ezekiel xxix. 3, “Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers.”
M. is very fond of this word, perhaps because *Saints* was the name by which many of the Republican Independents called themselves, in allusion to the sense ‘holy man’ in the Epistles of St Paul.
their readiest way from Succoth would have been by the north-east route, along the coast of the Mediterranean; but this would have brought them into the country of the warlike Philistines.

alluding to the “seventy of the elders of Israel,” whom Moses was directed to associate with himself in the government of the Israelites (Exod. xxiv., Numb. xi. 16–24), in which Council some scholars have seen the beginnings of the Jewish Sanhedrim.

some suppose that M. was thinking of the Temple and had forgotten that shittim-wood was employed in the construction of the Tabernacle. But may not M. have thought that the wood called shittim was some kind of cedar (though scholars now identify it with the acacia)?

referring to the two images of Cherubim, overlaid with gold, which were placed, with expanded wings, over the mercy-seat that covered the ark. The figures symbolised the guardian powers that drove off evil spirits.

lemma: So many laws argue so many sins
gloss: *argue so many sins*, prove so many sins to exist. The sentiment of the whole line is that expressed by Tacitus—*corruptissima republica plurimae leges*.

Deuteronomy xxxiv. The passage is well illustrated by *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 26: “The imperfection of the law was manifested in the person of Moses himself; for Moses, who was a type of the law, could not bring the children of Israel into the land of Canaan, that is, into eternal rest.”

lemma: But Joshua, whom the Gentiles Jesus call
gloss: Joshua, ‘the Saviour,’ is the same word as *Jesus*. Joshua is treated as a type of Christ (cf. Hebrews iv. 8), the points of resemblance being many. *quell*, crush utterly; a stronger word then.
the seventy years of Captivity, foretold by Jeremiah (xxv. 12), dated from B.C. 606 to B.C. 536.

an allusion to the struggle for the high-priesthood, in the 2nd cent. B.C., between Jason and Menelaus. The conflicts that arose between the rival high-priests gave Antiochus an excuse for assaulting Jerusalem and plundering the Temple, 170 B.C. Indirectly, lines 353–55 are an attack, like 507–37, on the clergy.

i.e. Antipater an Idumean (the Greek form of Edomite), who was made governor of Jerusalem by Pompey in 61 B.C. His second son was Herod the Great, who was appointed king of Judaea by the Roman Senate in 38 B.C. During his reign Christ was born.
*thither*, i.e. to Bethlehem; and M. speaks as though the song of the angels was heard there—not merely “in the field.” *squadroned*, in troops.

the literary form of the passage is primarily from Vergil, *Aeneid* I. 287, *Imperium oceano, famam qui terminet astris*. The theological idea is that of the “glorious reign of Christ on earth with his Saints, so often promised in Scripture, even until all his enemies shall be subdued” (*The Christian Doctrine*, I. 33).
deadly, fatal; cf. “my capital secret,” *S. A.* 394. Some editors think that in each passage there is a quibble on this and the other sense—‘pertaining to the head,’ Lat. *caput*.

“It is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree,” Gal. iii. 13. It was not only among the Jews that crucifixion was held in the utmost horror; the Romans regarded it as the greatest of degradations—a servile *supplicium* from which citizens and even freedmen were exempt.

“The enemies of Adam were the law that was against him, and the sins of all mankind as springing originally from him, and therefore in some sense chargeable upon him. The author, in this passage, alludes to Col. ii. 14” (Newton).

the “temporal death” of the redeemed is not an everlasting state, but a “sleep” from which there shall be an awakening (1 Cor. xv. 51). Milton discusses the question in *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 13, from which it is clear that by “temporal death” he signified the death of the body.
“It was the poet’s opinion that baptism should take place in running water” (Keightley). The passage in which M. expressed this view occurs in his treatise on *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 28.
this title of Satan is illustrated by *P. R.* I. 39–47, where he summons an assembly of his followers “in mid air.”
Ephes. vi. 11 (“put on the whole armour of God”), 13 and 16 (“to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked”).
it is St Paul’s favourite metaphor of athletes competing on the stadium (Heb. xii. 1; 1 Cor. ix. 24).

lemma: Wolves shall succeed for teachers, grievous wolves
gloss: “For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock,” Acts xx. 29. This passage (507–37), though it nominally traces the history of the Church from Apostolic times, is perhaps primarily directed against the Church of England.
“On this subject he had been particularly copious in his tract *Of Reformation in England*” (Todd). Compare Dante’s condemnation of the usurpation of temporal power by the Papacy.

lemma: in outward rites and specious forms
gloss: showing Milton’s dislike of ceremonies in worship.

lemma: till the day … Appear of respiration
gloss: there is an underlying political reference: M. never hesitates to foreshadow the ultimate overthrow of the Royalists against whom he and his party had struggled.

Matt. xxiv. 30; 2 Thess. i. 7, 8. See the end of the treatise *Of Reformation in England*, in which M. looks forward to “that day, when thou, the eternal and shortly-expected King, shalt open the clouds to judge the several kingdoms of the world.”
“This notion of the Heavens and Earth being renewed after the conflagration, and made the habitation of Angels and just men made perfect, was very pleasing to Milton” (Newton).
*Mors janua vitae*.

lemma: A Paradise within thee, happier far
gloss: the thought is anticipated in IV. 75, where Satan says of himself, “Which way I fly is hell: myself am hell.” It is one of those world-thoughts which occur independently to many minds.
cf. *Iliad* I. 63; “the application is very elegant in this place, as Adam’s was a vision, and Eve’s a dream; and God was in the one, as well as in the other” (Newton).
M. used the simile in IX. 179, 180, comparing Satan’s stealthy course through the garden to “a black mist low-creeping.” *marish*, marsh; an old word.

Dunster observed that the simile may be an echo of Sylvester’s *Du Bartas*, which speaks of the entrance to Eden as guarded by “A waving sword, whose body shined bright, Like flaming comet in the midst of night.”

lemma: In either hand the hastening Angel caught
gloss: a reminiscence of Gen. xix. 16, “And while he (Lot) lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife… and they brought him forth.”

lemma: The world was all before them
gloss: editors compare *Richard II*. I. 3. 206, 207 (Mowbray’s parting words): “Save back to England, all the world’s my way.”

This couplet has been much discussed since Addison proposed to omit it on the inadequate grounds that the lines strike a note of sadness, whereas an epic is supposed to require a cheerful ending. Their calm beauty is appropriate to the feeling of mingled resignation and reluctance with which we may suppose that the exiles left their Paradise.
